lessons.title: Tokyo
lessons.goal: Remember Tokyo as Japan’s capital and a major center of politics and business.

introductions.text:
Meet Tokyo, Japan’s capital.

Tokyo is Japan’s capital and a major center of politics and business. One of its landmarks is Tokyo Tower.

questions.prompt: What is Japan’s capital today?
questions.feedback: Tokyo is Japan’s capital today.

questions.prompt: Tokyo is a major center of politics and ___.
questions.feedback: Tokyo is a major center of politics and business.

questions.prompt: Tokyo has a landmark called Tokyo ___.
questions.feedback: The landmark is called Tokyo Tower.
questions.editor_note: Add “One of its landmarks is Tokyo Tower” to the introduction before this question. Corrects the original unrelated “That’s Tokyo!” feedback.

lessons.recap: Tokyo → Japan’s capital today; politics and business; Tokyo Tower.
lessons.editor_note: Three supplied questions are intentional in this handoff; do not duplicate or invent questions to reach six.

lessons.title: Kyoto
lessons.goal: Connect Kyoto with its historic capital identity and traditional culture.

introductions.text:
A thousand-year capital

Kyoto was Japan’s capital for more than 1,000 years. Tokyo is the capital today, but Kyoto remains an important center of traditional Japanese culture.

History in the streets

Some of Kyoto’s traditional streets feature wooden townhouses. These buildings are called machiya. They are one example of how Kyoto’s traditional culture remains visible today.

questions.prompt: Which city was Japan’s capital before Tokyo?
questions.feedback: Kyoto is Japan’s historic capital. Tokyo is the capital today.

questions.prompt: Kyoto served as Japan’s capital for more than ___.
questions.feedback: Kyoto was Japan’s capital for more than 1,000 years.

questions.prompt: What material are these traditional townhouses built from?
questions.feedback: These traditional townhouses are wooden buildings.
questions.editor_note: Keep the previously introduced machiya photo visible, as requested; this is supported observation, not unaided image recall.

questions.prompt: A machiya is a traditional wooden ___.
questions.feedback: A machiya is a traditional wooden townhouse.

questions.prompt: Which city did this lesson introduce for its traditional wooden townhouses?
questions.feedback: Kyoto’s traditional townhouses are part of its cultural landscape.

questions.prompt: Match each city with its capital identity.
questions.feedback: Tokyo is the capital today. Kyoto has a long history as a former capital.
questions.visual_direction: Text ↔ text. City names are clearer than generic city stickers.

lessons.recap: Kyoto → Japan’s historic capital for more than 1,000 years; traditional culture; wooden townhouses called machiya.

lessons.title: Osaka
lessons.goal: Connect Osaka’s commercial identity with its food-trading history.

introductions.text:
A city built on trade

Osaka is a major commercial city. Commerce means buying and selling goods. For centuries, merchants brought rice and other foods from across Japan to trade in Osaka.

The nation’s kitchen

With so much food passing through the city, Osaka became known as “the nation’s kitchen.” Today, food remains an important part of Osaka’s identity.

Remember: Osaka → Commerce and food culture.

questions.prompt: What does commerce mean?
questions.feedback: Commerce means buying and selling goods.

questions.prompt: Merchants brought food to Osaka to ___.
questions.feedback: Osaka was an important place for trading food from across Japan.

questions.prompt: Osaka became known as “the nation’s ___.”
questions.feedback: Osaka is known as the nation’s kitchen.

questions.prompt: What helped Osaka earn the nickname “the nation’s kitchen”?
questions.feedback: Food from across Japan was gathered and traded in Osaka.

questions.prompt: Which city introduced here is known for commerce and food culture?
questions.feedback: Food culture is an important part of Osaka’s identity.

questions.prompt: Match each city with its connection.
questions.feedback: Three cities, each with a different connection to remember!
questions.visual_direction: Text ↔ text. Keep the three city identities distinct.

lessons.recap: Osaka → major commercial city; historic food trade; the nation’s kitchen.

lessons.title: Mount Fuji
lessons.goal: Connect Mount Fuji’s height with its spiritual and artistic significance.

introductions.text:
Meet Mount Fuji

Mount Fuji is Japan’s highest mountain. It is also called Fujisan. Both names refer to the same mountain.

More than a mountain

For centuries, Mount Fuji has been a sacred place and an inspiration for artists. Its spiritual and artistic significance earned it recognition as a UNESCO Cultural World Heritage Site.

Remember: Mount Fuji → Highest mountain; spiritual meaning; art.

questions.prompt: Mount Fuji is Japan’s ___ mountain.
questions.feedback: Mount Fuji is Japan’s highest mountain.

questions.prompt: What does Fujisan refer to?
questions.feedback: Fujisan is another name for Mount Fuji.

questions.prompt: What type of UNESCO World Heritage Site is Mount Fuji?
questions.feedback: Its cultural recognition reflects its spiritual and artistic significance.

questions.prompt: Fuji has been a ___ and a source of ___.
questions.feedback: Mount Fuji has spiritual meaning and has inspired art.
questions.editor_note: Two ordered slots. First = sacred place; second = artistic inspiration. Replaces select-two.

questions.prompt: Is Mount Fuji important only because it is tall?
questions.feedback: Its cultural story matters too: spiritual significance and artistic inspiration.

questions.prompt: Match each place with its connection.
questions.feedback: You’ve connected a new landmark with the places you already know.
questions.visual_direction: Picture + name ↔ description for Fuji; text city names for Osaka and Kyoto. A Fuji photo or sticker can reinforce the landmark without making generic city art the clue.

lessons.recap: Mount Fuji → Japan’s highest mountain; also called Fujisan; UNESCO Cultural World Heritage Site.

lessons.title: Shinkansen
lessons.goal: Remember the Shinkansen as high-speed rail connecting major cities.

introductions.text:
Meet the Shinkansen

The Shinkansen is Japan’s high-speed railway system. Its trains are also called bullet trains. They carry passengers between major cities.

Connect your journey

Remember Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka? The Shinkansen connects these cities. It helps people travel between them for work or to explore Japan.

Remember: Shinkansen → High-speed travel between major cities.

Follow this sample itinerary: start in Tokyo, visit Kyoto next, then finish in Osaka. This is one example journey, not the only possible route.

questions.prompt: What is the Shinkansen?
questions.feedback: The Shinkansen is Japan’s high-speed railway system.

questions.prompt: Shinkansen trains are also called ___ trains.
questions.feedback: Shinkansen trains are also called bullet trains.

questions.prompt: The Shinkansen connects major ___.
questions.feedback: The Shinkansen connects major cities within Japan.

questions.prompt: Put the stops in this sample itinerary in order.
questions.feedback: This example journey starts in Tokyo, continues to Kyoto, and finishes in Osaka.
questions.visible_context: Follow this sample itinerary: start in Tokyo, visit Kyoto next, then finish in Osaka. This is one example journey, not the only possible route.
questions.editor_note: Add the itinerary to Introduction 2 before this question. Keep the itinerary visible for this beginner task, making it supported route-following rather than a claim about the only Shinkansen route. Shuffle the city cards.

questions.prompt: Which one is a transport system?
questions.feedback: Shinkansen is the railway system. Mount Fuji is a mountain, and Osaka is a city.

questions.prompt: Match all five names with their connections.
questions.feedback: You’ve connected all five ideas from this unit!
questions.visual_direction: Round A: text city names ↔ identities. Round B: Fuji sticker + name / Shinkansen sticker + name ↔ mountain / railway descriptions. Introduce both stickers alongside their names before this review.
questions.editor_note: Two rounds within one question: Round A cities (3 pairs); Round B Fuji and Shinkansen (2 pairs). Only complete the question after both rounds.

lessons.recap: Shinkansen → high-speed railway; bullet trains; connects major cities including Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka.

lessons.title: Shibuya
lessons.goal: Connect Shibuya with its crossing, entertainment, and Hachiko meeting point.

introductions.text: Shibuya is a lively district in Tokyo, known for shopping and entertainment. Its famous **Scramble Crossing** lets pedestrians cross in several directions, including diagonally, when the pedestrian signals allow it.

Near Shibuya Station stands a statue of **Hachiko**, a dog remembered for his loyalty. The statue is a well-known meeting point. Connect the two landmarks: **crossing for walking, Hachiko for meeting**.

questions.prompt: Shibuya is a district in which city?
questions.feedback: Shibuya is part of Tokyo.

questions.prompt: At the Scramble Crossing, people can walk straight across or ___.
questions.feedback: The crossing allows several directions, including diagonal routes.

questions.prompt: You want a lively area for shopping and entertainment. Which place fits this introduction?
questions.feedback: Shopping and entertainment are part of Shibuya's identity.

questions.prompt: What animal does the Hachiko statue show?
questions.feedback: Hachiko was a dog remembered for his loyalty.

questions.prompt: What should you look for at the Hachiko meeting point?
questions.feedback: The Hachiko statue is a familiar meeting point near Shibuya Station.

questions.prompt: Connect each Shibuya landmark with its role.
questions.feedback: The crossing and the statue are two different Shibuya landmarks.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ role: Scramble Crossing photo + name / Hachiko photo + name. Photos must already appear with the names in introductions.

lessons.recap: Shibuya → Tokyo district; Scramble Crossing → several crossing directions; Hachiko → dog statue and meeting point.

lessons.title: Asakusa and Senso-ji
lessons.goal: Distinguish a Tokyo neighborhood, its temple, and its approach.

introductions.text: **Asakusa** is a historic neighborhood in Tokyo. **Senso-ji** is a Buddhist temple in Asakusa—and Tokyo's oldest temple. Remember: **Asakusa is the area; Senso-ji is the temple**.

The **Kaminarimon**, or Thunder Gate, is a famous entrance associated with Senso-ji. Beyond it, **Nakamise** is a shopping street on the approach to the temple. It has shops selling snacks and souvenirs.

On this approach, pass through Kaminarimon, walk along Nakamise, then continue toward Senso-ji’s main hall.

questions.prompt: Which name refers to the neighborhood?
questions.feedback: Asakusa is the neighborhood containing Senso-ji.

questions.prompt: Senso-ji is a Buddhist ___.
questions.feedback: Senso-ji is a Buddhist temple.

questions.prompt: Senso-ji is a temple in the neighborhood of ___.
questions.feedback: Senso-ji is the temple, and Asakusa is the surrounding area.
questions.editor_note: Restates the original area–temple relationship without long answer sentences.

questions.prompt: What is Kaminarimon?
questions.feedback: Kaminarimon is the Thunder Gate.

questions.prompt: Put these stops on the approach to Senso-ji in order.
questions.feedback: This approach goes through Kaminarimon, along Nakamise, and toward the main hall.
questions.editor_note: Add the short route sentence to Introduction 2. These are selected stops along the approach, not an exhaustive list of every gate. Do not number the cards before the learner arranges them.

questions.prompt: Match the three names with their meanings.
questions.feedback: The area, temple, and street each have their own name.
questions.visual_direction: Mixed cards + name ↔ category: text “Asakusa”; Senso-ji photo + name; Nakamise street photo + name. Do not imply a neighborhood can be uniquely recognized from a generic street photo.

lessons.recap: Asakusa → historic Tokyo neighborhood; Senso-ji → Buddhist temple; Kaminarimon → gate; Nakamise → shopping street.

lessons.title: Tokyo Skytree
lessons.goal: Remember the tower’s height and its two main functions.

introductions.text: **Tokyo Skytree** is a **634-meter tower** in Tokyo. It is a broadcasting tower: it helps transmit television signals. Its height is measured to the top of the tower.
Skytree also has **observation decks**—places high up where visitors look out over the city. The tower therefore has two roles: **broadcasting signals and offering city views**.

questions.prompt: What kind of landmark is Tokyo Skytree?
questions.feedback: Tokyo Skytree is a tower in Tokyo.

questions.prompt: Tokyo Skytree is ___ meters tall.
questions.feedback: Its total height is 634 meters.

questions.prompt: What does Skytree help broadcast?
questions.feedback: Broadcasting is one of Skytree's main functions.

questions.prompt: Where can visitors look out over Tokyo from Skytree?
questions.feedback: Observation decks are designed for visitors to enjoy the view.

questions.prompt: Skytree provides ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: Skytree combines broadcasting and sightseeing.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles. Replaces the original select-two interaction; preserves both functions.

questions.prompt: Match the Tokyo landmarks with their features.
questions.feedback: Tokyo's landmarks have different purposes and visual clues.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ feature: Skytree, Senso-ji, Shibuya Crossing. Include each visible name so the task still tests the original feature relationship.

lessons.recap: Tokyo Skytree → 634 meters; broadcasting; observation decks. Decks are below the tower’s total height.

sources.title: Tokyo Skytree operator: height and facilities

lessons.title: Meiji Jingu
lessons.goal: Identify the shrine, whom it honors, and its planted forest.

introductions.text: **Meiji Jingu** is a **Shinto shrine in Tokyo**. It honors **Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken**. A shrine is a place of worship; you will explore Shinto in a later unit.

A large forest surrounds Meiji Jingu. Although it can look like a natural woodland, people **planted and planned the forest**. Trees were donated from across Japan to help create the shrine's setting.

questions.prompt: What kind of place is Meiji Jingu?
questions.feedback: Meiji Jingu is a Shinto shrine.

questions.prompt: Meiji Jingu honors ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: The shrine is dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles. Keep each full title/name in one tile; do not split Japanese names into words.

questions.prompt: Which city contains Meiji Jingu?
questions.feedback: Meiji Jingu is in Tokyo.

questions.prompt: What surrounds Meiji Jingu?
questions.feedback: A large forest surrounds the shrine.

questions.prompt: People ___ the forest around Meiji Jingu.
questions.feedback: People planted and planned the forest.

questions.prompt: Connect each place with its main identity.
questions.feedback: Remember the function as well as the name.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ identity: Meiji Jingu, Senso-ji, Skytree. Use prior introduction images.

lessons.recap: Meiji Jingu → Tokyo Shinto shrine; Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken; a forest planted by people.

lessons.title: Kiyomizu-dera
lessons.goal: Recognize the wooden stage and the water behind the name.

introductions.text: **Kiyomizu-dera** is a Buddhist temple in **Kyoto**. It is famous for a large **wooden stage** projecting from its main hall over the hillside. Visitors can look out toward the city from the stage.
The name **Kiyomizu** means **“pure water.”** It refers to the **Otowa Waterfall** at the temple. The water and the wooden stage give you two different ways to remember this place.

questions.prompt: In which city is Kiyomizu-dera?
questions.feedback: Kiyomizu-dera is in Kyoto.

questions.prompt: Which feature is Kiyomizu-dera famous for?
questions.feedback: Its wooden stage is the landmark's key visual feature.

questions.prompt: A photograph shows a temple platform extending over a hillside. Which lesson's landmark fits?
questions.feedback: The projecting wooden stage is the clue.

questions.prompt: Kiyomizu means “___.”
questions.feedback: Kiyomizu means pure water.

questions.prompt: The temple's name connects with a ___.
questions.feedback: The name refers to the water of Otowa Waterfall.

questions.prompt: Match each place with its feature.
questions.feedback: Use a distinctive feature to recall each place.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ feature: Kiyomizu-dera stage, Skytree, Senso-ji. Each photo must show the relevant site clearly.

lessons.recap: Kiyomizu-dera → Kyoto Buddhist temple; wooden stage; “pure water” and Otowa Waterfall.

lessons.title: Kinkaku-ji
lessons.goal: Connect the Golden Pavilion with real gold leaf and its pond setting.

introductions.text: **Kinkaku-ji** is a Buddhist temple in **Kyoto**, famous for its **Golden Pavilion**. The pavilion's upper two floors are covered in **gold leaf**—very thin sheets of real gold.
The Golden Pavilion stands beside a **pond**, where its reflection can be seen. Compare Kyoto's two landmarks: **Kinkaku-ji has the golden pavilion; Kiyomizu-dera has the wooden stage**.

questions.prompt: Which city is home to Kinkaku-ji?
questions.feedback: Kinkaku-ji is a Kyoto temple.

questions.prompt: Its famous pavilion is known as the ___ Pavilion.
questions.feedback: The Golden Pavilion gives Kinkaku-ji its familiar identity.

questions.prompt: What covers the pavilion’s upper floors?
questions.feedback: Thin sheets of gold cover the upper two floors.

questions.prompt: Where can the pavilion’s reflection be seen?
questions.feedback: The pond is part of the pavilion's famous setting.

questions.prompt: Your photo shows a golden building beside water. Which landmark fits?
questions.feedback: Gold-covered upper floors and the pond are the clues.

questions.prompt: Match the two Kyoto temples with their features.
questions.feedback: Both are temples, but their memorable features differ.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ feature: Kinkaku-ji golden pavilion and Kiyomizu-dera wooden stage.

lessons.recap: Kinkaku-ji → Kyoto; Golden Pavilion; real gold leaf on upper floors; reflection in a pond.

lessons.title: Fushimi Inari Taisha
lessons.goal: Recognize its torii paths, offerings, and fox messengers.

introductions.text: **Fushimi Inari Taisha** is a Shinto shrine in **Kyoto**. It is famous for thousands of **vermilion torii gates** along its paths. Vermilion is a bright red-orange color; torii are gateways associated with Shinto sacred spaces.

The gates are **offerings**, given in connection with prayers and thanks. You may also notice **fox statues**: foxes are regarded as messengers of Inari. The shrine explains that **Inari is not a fox**.

questions.prompt: What kind of place is Fushimi Inari Taisha?
questions.feedback: Fushimi Inari Taisha is a Shinto shrine in Kyoto.

questions.prompt: Which feature is Fushimi Inari famous for?
questions.feedback: Rows of torii are its defining visual feature.

questions.prompt: Vermilion is a bright ___ color.
questions.feedback: The gates' red-orange color is called vermilion.

questions.prompt: The torii gates were offered with ___.
questions.feedback: The gates have a religious purpose beyond their appearance.
questions.editor_note: One phrase tile represents the religious purpose; do not require assembling an entire sentence.

questions.prompt: What do the fox figures represent?
questions.feedback: Foxes are regarded as Inari's messengers, not Inari itself.

questions.prompt: Connect the Kyoto landmarks with their clues.
questions.feedback: Each landmark has a different visual connection.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ clue: Fushimi Inari torii paths; Kinkaku-ji golden pavilion; Kiyomizu-dera stage.

lessons.recap: Fushimi Inari Taisha → Kyoto shrine; vermilion torii; offerings; fox messengers.

lessons.title: Gion
lessons.goal: Identify Gion as a living district associated with traditional performers.

introductions.text:
**Gion** is a historic district in **Kyoto**. It is associated with **geiko and maiko**, traditional performers. A **geiko** is a trained professional; a **maiko** is an apprentice learning the profession.

A maiko is an apprentice who trains before becoming a fully trained geiko.

Gion is a **living neighborhood**, not a stage set. People live and work there. If you see geiko or maiko walking, give them space: **do not stop, follow, or photograph them without permission**. Detailed performing arts come in a later unit.

questions.prompt: What kind of place is Gion?
questions.feedback: Gion is an area of Kyoto, rather than a single landmark building.

questions.prompt: What is a maiko?
questions.feedback: A maiko is training in the profession.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the profession in order, starting with the apprentice.
questions.feedback: Maiko is the apprentice stage; geiko is the trained professional.
questions.editor_note: Add the progression sentence to Introduction 1 before Q3. Use two text cards. Do not require costume-based identification or invent a third training stage.

questions.prompt: A maiko walks past on her way to work. What should you do?
questions.feedback: Respect people working and living in Gion.

questions.prompt: Gion is a ___ where people live and work.
questions.feedback: Gion is part of everyday Kyoto as well as a historic district.
questions.editor_note: Preserves the distinction between a living district and a stage set.

questions.prompt: Match each Kyoto place with its identity.
questions.feedback: Distinguish the district from the temple and shrine.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + name ↔ identity. Use an introduced Gion streetscape, Kinkaku-ji, and Fushimi Inari. Names stay visible to avoid ambiguous street-image identification.

lessons.recap: Gion → Kyoto historic district; geiko and maiko; respect residents and working performers.

lessons.title: Shinto
lessons.goal: Understand kami, nature, and the role of ritual practices.

introductions.text: **Shinto** is a religious tradition that developed in Japan. It centers on **kami**—sacred beings or presences. Kami can be associated with **nature**, such as mountains and trees, and with **ancestors**.

Respect and gratitude toward kami are important in Shinto. **Rituals** are meaningful, repeated practices. Shinto includes practices of **purification**, or ritual cleansing, and offerings to kami. These are religious practices, not scientific claims about nature.

questions.prompt: Where did Shinto develop?
questions.feedback: Shinto developed in Japan.

questions.prompt: Sacred beings or presences in Shinto are called ___.
questions.feedback: Kami is a key word for understanding Shinto.

questions.prompt: Kami can be associated with ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: Kami can be associated with nature and ancestors.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles.

questions.prompt: What does purification mean here?
questions.feedback: Purification is a ritual practice connected with cleanliness and preparation.

questions.prompt: People give thanks to kami for nature’s blessings. Which tradition fits?
questions.feedback: Giving thanks to kami is part of Shinto practice.

questions.prompt: Which place you learned about is a Shinto shrine?
questions.feedback: Meiji Jingu is an example of a Shinto shrine.

lessons.recap: Shinto → Japan; kami; nature and ancestors; respect, gratitude, and ritual practices.

lessons.title: Buddhism
lessons.goal: Recognize its Indian origins, Buddha connection, and influence in Japan.

introductions.text: **Buddhism** began in ancient **India** and is based on the teachings of the **Buddha**. Its teachings include developing wisdom and compassion—understanding and care for others. It spread across Asia before reaching Japan.

Buddhism reached Japan in the **sixth century**, more than 1,000 years ago, through the Korean Peninsula. It influenced Japanese **art and architecture**, including religious statues and temple buildings. Shinto and Buddhism have also influenced one another over time; people may take part in both traditions.

questions.prompt: Where did Buddhism begin?
questions.feedback: Buddhism began in ancient India.

questions.prompt: Buddhism is based on the teachings of the ___.
questions.feedback: The Buddha's teachings are central to Buddhism.

questions.prompt: Someone tries to understand another person's suffering and respond with care. Which teaching does this illustrate?
questions.feedback: Compassion means responding to others with care.

questions.prompt: Through which area did Buddhism reach Japan?
questions.feedback: Buddhism reached Japan through the Korean Peninsula in the sixth century.

questions.prompt: Buddhism influenced Japanese ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: Buddhism has influenced Japanese art and architecture.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles.

questions.prompt: Match the traditions with their origins.
questions.feedback: They have different origins and a long history of interaction in Japan.
questions.visual_direction: Text ↔ text. Origins are conceptual relationships, not picture-recognition tasks.

lessons.recap: Buddhism → Buddha; ancient India; compassion and wisdom; influence on Japanese art and architecture.

sources.title: India Embassy in Tokyo: cultural exchange
Metropolitan Museum: Buddhism and Buddhist Art
Metropolitan Museum: Buddhist teachings and art

lessons.title: Shinto Shrines
lessons.goal: Connect shrines with kami and common visitor features.

introductions.text: A **Shinto shrine** is a sacred place where **kami are honored**. Another word for a shrine is **jinja**. Shrines may be large or small; their purpose is religious, not just sightseeing.

A shrine entrance is often marked by a **torii gate**. Many shrines also have a **water basin for purification** before worship. Follow the instructions at the site; arrangements and customs can differ.

A common shrine visit follows this order: pass through the torii, cleanse at the purification basin, then pay respects to the kami. Follow instructions at the individual shrine.

questions.prompt: Who are honored at Shinto shrines?
questions.feedback: Shinto shrines are places for honoring kami.

questions.prompt: Jinja means ___.
questions.feedback: Jinja is another word for a Shinto shrine.

questions.prompt: Meiji Jingu and Fushimi Inari are ___.
questions.feedback: Both places are examples of Shinto shrines.
questions.editor_note: Replaces the long paired-name answer choices; both named sites were taught earlier.

questions.prompt: Which gateway is especially associated with a Shinto shrine?
questions.feedback: A torii is a familiar marker of Shinto sacred space.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a common shrine visit in order.
questions.feedback: The common sequence is entrance, purification, then paying respects. Follow the shrine’s own instructions.
questions.editor_note: Add the sequence to Introduction 2 before Q5. Teach this as a common pattern, not a universal requirement at every site. Source: Jinja Honcho’s Entering a Jinja page.

questions.prompt: People are praying at a shrine. Treat it as a ___.
questions.feedback: Shrines are living religious spaces, even when visitors also come to sightsee.
questions.editor_note: Short answer choices; preserves respectful visitor behavior.

lessons.recap: Shrine / jinja → honoring kami; torii entrance; purification basin at many sites.

lessons.title: Buddhist Temples
lessons.goal: Recognize temples as Buddhist religious spaces with varied features.

introductions.text: A **Buddhist temple** is a place for Buddhist worship and practice. Temples may contain images of the **Buddha and other revered Buddhist figures**. Senso-ji, Kiyomizu-dera, and Kinkaku-ji are examples you already know.

At many temples, visitors offer **incense**—fragrant material that gives off smoke when burned. Quiet prayer with **palms together** is common. Not every temple looks the same, and local instructions matter more than a single visual clue.

questions.prompt: Which religion is connected with a Buddhist temple?
questions.feedback: Buddhist temples are places for Buddhist worship and practice.

questions.prompt: Senso-ji and Kiyomizu-dera are ___.
questions.feedback: Both are Buddhist temples introduced in earlier lessons.
questions.editor_note: Replaces select-two while retaining both temple examples.

questions.prompt: Temple images may depict ___.
questions.feedback: Buddhist images are part of many temples' religious life.
questions.editor_note: Do not imply every statue depicts the historical Buddha; the original introduction also includes other Buddhist figures.

questions.prompt: What gives off fragrant smoke when burned as an offering?
questions.feedback: Incense is offered at many Buddhist temples.

questions.prompt: Which action fits quiet prayer at a Buddhist temple?
questions.feedback: Quiet prayer with palms together is common at temples.

questions.prompt: Connect each kind of site with its tradition.
questions.feedback: The basic distinction helps you understand the sites, even where histories overlap.
questions.visual_direction: Photo + explicit site name ↔ religion: Meiji Jingu / Senso-ji. Introduce these as examples, and use each religion label once. Not a universal appearance-only test for shrine versus temple.
questions.editor_note: Use previously taught named examples instead of generic site-type labels; the original shrine/temple distinction remains the goal.

lessons.recap: Buddhist temples → worship and practice; Buddhist images; incense and quiet prayer at many sites.

sources.title: Nara official: shrine and temple manners
Aichi official: temple and shrine etiquette

lessons.title: Torii Gates
lessons.goal: Recognize the gateway’s form, meaning, and variety.

introductions.text: A **torii** is a gateway marking entry to a **Shinto sacred space**. Its familiar form has **two upright posts joined by crosspieces**. Passing through marks a transition into a place treated with religious respect.
Torii are **not all red**. Some are unpainted wood or stone. At **Fushimi Inari Taisha**, rows of vermilion torii make a famous scene. Remember the gateway's **meaning**, not just its color.

questions.prompt: A torii marks entry to what kind of space?
questions.feedback: A torii marks a sacred boundary.

questions.prompt: A familiar torii shape has two upright ___ joined by crosspieces.
questions.feedback: Two upright posts and crosspieces form the familiar gateway shape.

questions.prompt: Passing through a torii marks entry into a ___.
questions.feedback: The gateway carries religious meaning, rather than being only decoration.

questions.prompt: Can a torii be unpainted wood?
questions.feedback: Torii can have different materials and colors.

questions.prompt: Which Kyoto shrine is known for rows of vermilion torii?
questions.feedback: Fushimi Inari's torii paths are a memorable example.

questions.prompt: A torii marks Shinto ___ and may be made of ___.
questions.feedback: Meaning and form matter more than one particular color.
questions.editor_note: Two ordered slots: first = sacred space, second = stone. Bank contains four separate tiles. Preserves both original correct statements.

lessons.recap: Torii → sacred gateway; posts and crosspieces; different materials and colors; familiar at Fushimi Inari.

sources.title: Jinja Honcho: Torii structure and materials

lessons.title: Sushi
lessons.goal: Recognize vinegared rice and avoid the raw-fish-only misconception.

introductions.text: **Sushi** combines **vinegared rice** with ingredients such as seafood, vegetables, or egg. Vinegared rice is rice seasoned with vinegar. The rice—not raw fish alone—is the key connection.
Sushi ingredients can be **raw or cooked**. **Sashimi** is sliced raw seafood served without sushi rice; it is a different dish. **Raw seafood alone does not make something sushi.**

questions.prompt: Which ingredient is central to sushi?
questions.feedback: Seasoned, vinegared rice is central to sushi.

questions.prompt: Sushi can include ___ or ___ alongside its rice.
questions.feedback: Sushi can include vegetables or egg as well as seafood.

lessons.title: Ramen
lessons.goal: Recognize wheat noodles, broth, toppings, and Chinese influences.

introductions.text: **Ramen** is a Japanese noodle dish that developed from **Chinese noodle influences**. A typical bowl contains **wheat noodles in broth**. Broth means the flavorful soup surrounding the noodles.

Ramen bowls often have **toppings**, such as egg, vegetables, or sliced meat. The **broth, noodles, and toppings can vary**. Ramen is not one identical recipe; regional versions will come in a later unit.

questions.prompt: What are ramen noodles usually made from?

lessons.recap: Ramen → Chinese influences; wheat noodles; broth; varied toppings.

lessons.title: Tempura
lessons.goal: Connect seafood and vegetables with batter and deep-frying.

introductions.text: **Tempura** is seafood or vegetables coated in **batter** and **deep-fried**. Batter is a wet flour mixture. Deep-frying cooks the coated ingredients in hot oil, creating a crisp outside.

Tempura can include **shrimp** or vegetables such as **sweet potato and eggplant**. It does not have to contain seafood. What links these examples is the **batter-and-frying method**.

For tempura, prepare seafood or vegetables, coat them in batter, then deep-fry them.

questions.prompt: How is tempura cooked?
questions.feedback: Tempura is cooked in hot oil.

questions.prompt: The ingredients are coated in ___ before frying.
questions.feedback: Batter creates the coating around the ingredients.

questions.feedback: Batter is the wet mixture used to coat tempura.

questions.feedback: Both seafood and vegetables can be made into tempura.

lessons.title: Washoku
lessons.goal: Understand a food culture centered on seasons and nature.

introductions.text: **Washoku** means traditional Japanese food culture. It is **more than one dish**: it includes knowledge, skills, and customs connected with preparing and sharing food. Respect for **nature** is an important part of it.

Washoku values **seasonality**: ingredients and presentation can reflect the time of year. Seasonal flowers, leaves, or tableware can help express that connection. The goal is to notice the link between **food, seasons, and nature**.

questions.prompt: What does washoku describe?
questions.feedback: Washoku is broader than an individual dish.

questions.prompt: Food culture includes ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: Washoku includes practices and knowledge around food.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles.

questions.prompt: An important connection in washoku is respect for ___.
questions.feedback: Respect for nature is part of washoku.

questions.prompt: Choosing ingredients and presentation for the time of year expresses ___.
questions.feedback: Seasonality connects a meal with its time of year.
questions.editor_note: The next question applies this meaning to a meal rather than repeating the definition.

questions.feedback: Ingredients and presentation can both reflect the season.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a broader food culture rather than one dish?
questions.feedback: Sushi and tempura are dishes; washoku describes a broader culture.

lessons.recap: Washoku → traditional food culture; skills and customs; seasons; respect for nature.

lessons.title: Izakaya
lessons.goal: Recognize a casual dining venue with drinks and shared dishes.

introductions.text: An **izakaya** is a casual Japanese place serving **drinks and a variety of dishes**. It is a **type of establishment**, not the name of one food. People often visit with friends or colleagues.
Dishes at an izakaya are often ordered **to share**. A group can try several plates together. You do not have to drink alcohol: many izakaya also offer **nonalcoholic drinks**.

questions.prompt: What is an izakaya?
questions.feedback: Izakaya names a kind of dining establishment.

questions.prompt: An izakaya serves ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: Food and drinks are both part of an izakaya visit.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles.

questions.feedback: Izakaya are informal dining places.

questions.feedback: Shared dishes and drinks fit izakaya dining.

questions.feedback: Many izakaya offer nonalcoholic drinks too.

questions.feedback: These terms describe different parts of eating in Japan.

lessons.title: Emperor
lessons.goal: Separate Japan’s imperial institution from the emperor’s present constitutional role.

introductions.text: Japan has a **hereditary monarchy**: the position of emperor passes within the imperial family under succession rules. The emperor is different from the **prime minister**, who leads the government. The emperor's actual political power has changed across history.

Under Japan's current Constitution, the emperor is the **symbol of the state and the unity of the people**. The emperor carries out constitutional and ceremonial duties but has **no powers related to government**.

questions.prompt: In a hereditary monarchy, the position passes within the ___.
questions.feedback: Hereditary succession takes place within the imperial family under established rules.
questions.editor_note: Preserve “under succession rules” in the introduction and original feedback; no new succession detail is being taught.

questions.prompt: Who leads Japan's government today?
questions.feedback: The prime minister leads the government; the emperor has a different role.

questions.prompt: Which Tokyo shrine honors an emperor and an empress?
questions.feedback: Meiji Jingu honors Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken.

questions.prompt: Today, the emperor is a ___ of the state and the unity of the people.
questions.feedback: The Constitution defines the emperor's symbolic position.

questions.prompt: Does the emperor decide government policy today?
questions.feedback: The emperor has no powers related to government under the Constitution.
questions.editor_note: Original factual correction is retained in feedback; the title is not being compared with the prime minister’s powers in every historical era.

questions.prompt: Match the present-day roles.
questions.feedback: Keep the imperial role separate from the government's leadership.
questions.visual_direction: Text ↔ text. Emperor / prime minister roles are clearer than invented portrait stickers.

lessons.recap: Emperor → imperial family; historical role changed over time; today a constitutional symbol, not head of government.

lessons.title: Samurai
lessons.goal: Recognize the warrior class and its military, service, and cultural roles.

introductions.text: The **samurai** were Japan's historical **warrior class**. Many served powerful regional lords called **daimyo**. They trained in military skills and are often associated with swords and armor.

Samurai life was **not only fighting**. Some samurai also worked as administrators and practiced arts such as **poetry and calligraphy**. Their work changed with the times, especially during long periods of peace.

questions.feedback: Samurai were part of Japan's historical warrior class.

lessons.title: Shogun
lessons.goal: Understand the military leader’s position and distinguish it from the emperor.

introductions.text: A **shogun** was a military leader who headed a **warrior government** in Japanese history. During long periods of shogun rule, the shogun held much of the practical governing power. A shogun was a leader, not the name for all samurai.

The **emperor and shogun were different roles**. An emperor could remain in place while a shogun governed. **Kyoto** was associated with the imperial court; later, the Tokugawa shoguns based their government in **Edo**, today's Tokyo.

questions.prompt: What role did a shogun hold?
questions.feedback: Shogun was a leadership title.

questions.feedback: Shoguns held major military and governing authority.

questions.feedback: The emperor and shogun were different positions that could coexist.

questions.feedback: Their government was based in Edo.

questions.feedback: The distinctions help you read historical stories more clearly.

lessons.title: Shogunate
lessons.goal: Distinguish the leader from the government and connect national and regional rule.

introductions.text: A **shogunate** was a government led by a shogun. Remember the distinction: **shogun = leader; shogunate = government**. It involved officials and systems of rule, not just one person's actions.

The **Tokugawa shogunate** was one historical example. Its central government was based in **Edo**. Regional lords, or **daimyo**, governed their domains under the shogunate's authority. This connected central power with regional government.

questions.feedback: A shogunate was the government headed by a shogun.

lessons.title: Edo Period
lessons.goal: Connect the period with Tokugawa rule and the city now called Tokyo.

introductions.text: The **Edo period** is the period of Tokugawa rule, conventionally dated **1603–1868**. It lasted more than 250 years. **Edo** was the name of the city now called **Tokyo**.

Edo grew as the shogunate's government center, while **Kyoto remained the home of the imperial court**. Tokugawa rule ended in **1868**, when Japan's governing system changed. The details of that change belong to a later history unit.

lessons.title: Pacific War
lessons.goal: Place the 1941–1945 conflict within World War II without erasing earlier war in Asia.

introductions.text: The **Pacific War** was part of World War II. Here, the term refers to the **1941–1945** war between Japan and the United States and other Allied powers across the Pacific and parts of Asia. **Japan's war in China had already begun earlier**; war in Asia did not start everywhere in 1941.

In **December 1941**, Japanese forces attacked **Pearl Harbor**, a U.S. naval base in Hawaii. The United States then entered World War II. Fighting in the Pacific and Asia affected military personnel and civilians across many countries.

questions.feedback: The Pacific War formed part of World War II.

questions.feedback: This lesson uses 1941–1945 for the Pacific War.

questions.feedback: Yes. Japan’s war in China had already begun before 1941.
questions.editor_note: Reverses the yes/no wording to retain the important earlier-war distinction with short answer choices. Update feedback to “Yes. Japan’s war in China had already begun before 1941.”

lessons.title: Hiroshima Atomic Bombing
lessons.goal: Remember the date, the first wartime nuclear attack, and its human consequences.

introductions.text: On **August 6, 1945**, the **United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima**. It was the first use of a nuclear weapon in war. Hiroshima is a Japanese city; this event occurred near the end of World War II.

The bombing caused widespread destruction and loss of life. Survivors faced lasting consequences, including illness linked to radiation. Learning about Hiroshima means remembering **people's lives and experiences**, as well as the date.

questions.prompt: On which date was Hiroshima atomically bombed?
questions.feedback: Hiroshima was bombed on August 6, 1945.

questions.prompt: Which country dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima?
questions.feedback: The United States carried out the atomic bombing.

questions.prompt: Hiroshima was the first use of a nuclear weapon in ___.
questions.feedback: It was the first wartime use of a nuclear weapon.

questions.prompt: Did the effects continue after the day of the bombing?
questions.feedback: Yes. Survivors faced lasting consequences after August 6, including serious health effects.
questions.editor_note: Rephrased to avoid paragraph-length yes/no options; preserve the long-term consequences in feedback.

questions.prompt: The bombing caused ___ and ___.
questions.feedback: The event had both immediate and long-term human consequences.
questions.editor_note: Two blanks. Accept either order for the two correct tiles.

questions.prompt: Put the events in order.
questions.feedback: The two events occurred at different stages of the war.
questions.editor_note: Shuffle the event cards initially. Order from earliest to latest. Avoid printing dates that give away the answer.

lessons.recap: Hiroshima → August 6, 1945; U.S. atomic bombing; first wartime nuclear attack; immediate and lasting human suffering.

lessons.title: Nagasaki Atomic Bombing
lessons.goal: Remember the second city’s date and connect the two bombings in sequence.

introductions.text: On **August 9, 1945**, the **United States dropped an atomic bomb on Nagasaki**. This was **three days after Hiroshima**. Nagasaki was the second city attacked with an atomic bomb in war.

The Nagasaki bombing caused devastating loss of life and lasting suffering. Today, the city preserves records of the bombing and survivors' experiences. These records help people learn about what happened and the human consequences of nuclear weapons.

questions.prompt: Which city was atomically bombed on August 9, 1945?
questions.feedback: Nagasaki was bombed on August 9, 1945.

questions.feedback: Hiroshima came first, followed by Nagasaki three days later.

questions.feedback: Personal accounts help explain how the bombing affected people's lives.

lessons.title: End of World War II
lessons.goal: Distinguish surrender terms, the public announcement, and formal signing.

introductions.text: In **August 1945**, Japan accepted the terms of the **Potsdam Declaration**, which called for its surrender. Japan's acceptance was publicly announced in a radio broadcast on **August 15**. These events were part of the end of World War II.

The **formal surrender document** was signed on **September 2, 1945**, aboard the **USS Missouri** in Tokyo Bay. Remember the distinction: **August announcement; September formal signing**. These are separate events, not conflicting dates.

questions.feedback: Japan accepted the terms of the Potsdam Declaration in August 1945.

questions.feedback: The acceptance concerned surrender terms.

questions.feedback: The public radio announcement was on August 15, 1945.

questions.prompt: When was the formal surrender document signed?
questions.feedback: The formal signing was on September 2, 1945.

questions.prompt: On which ship was the formal surrender signed?
questions.feedback: The signing took place on the USS Missouri.
questions.editor_note: The stem specifies the ship; keep Tokyo Bay in feedback. Other names are distractors, not new learning targets.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order.
questions.feedback: Acceptance, announcement, and formal signing were distinct steps.
questions.editor_note: Shuffle the event cards initially. Order from earliest to latest. Avoid printing dates that give away the answer.

lessons.recap: End of war → Potsdam surrender terms accepted in August; August 15 announcement; September 2 formal signing on USS Missouri.

lessons.title: Atomic Bomb Dome
lessons.goal: Recognize the preserved ruin as evidence, remembrance, and a cultural heritage site.

introductions.text: The **Atomic Bomb Dome** stands in **Hiroshima**. It is the damaged remains of a building that stood near the 1945 bombing's hypocenter—the point on the ground beneath the explosion. Part of its structure remained standing.

The Dome is preserved as evidence of destruction and as a symbol of hope for **lasting peace and the elimination of nuclear weapons**. It became a **UNESCO Cultural World Heritage Site in 1996**. It is also called the **Hiroshima Peace Memorial**.

questions.prompt: In which city is the Atomic Bomb Dome?
questions.feedback: The Dome is in Hiroshima.

questions.prompt: The Dome preserves a building damaged by the ___.
questions.feedback: It is preserved physical evidence of the bombing.

questions.prompt: The hypocenter is the point on the ground ___ the explosion.
questions.feedback: The hypocenter lies beneath an explosion in the air.

questions.prompt: Why is the Dome preserved?
questions.feedback: The site links evidence of devastation with a message of peace.

questions.prompt: What is another name for the Atomic Bomb Dome?
questions.feedback: Hiroshima Peace Memorial is another name for the Atomic Bomb Dome.

questions.prompt: The Dome is in ___ and is a UNESCO ___ World Heritage Site.
questions.feedback: The damaged structure predates its 1996 World Heritage inscription.

lessons.recap: Atomic Bomb Dome → Hiroshima Peace Memorial; preserved damaged structure; evidence and peace; cultural World Heritage since 1996.
